narrative.text: ResearchGate cover page for the chapter "SWOT Analysis" (January 2015, DOI 10.1002/9781118785317.weom120103) by Tanya Sammut-Bonnici (University of Malta) and David Galea, showing citation and read counts, author profile links and related projects (Network Economy; Wiley Encyclopedia – Strategic Management). It notes that the content was uploaded by Sammut-Bonnici on 30 October 2017.

First page of the Wiley Encyclopedia of Management entry "SWOT analysis" by Sammut-Bonnici and Galea. A SWOT analysis assesses internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats so that an organisation can formulate its strategy; the article offers templates and practical guidance. Internal analysis identifies the source of competitive advantage: resources (tangible, such as raw materials and machinery, or intangible, such as finance, technology, human capital, patents and brand equity) combine into capabilities, which in turn yield core competencies that, if unique, give sustainable advantage and are hard for rivals to imitate. The internal resources fall into functional categories (financial, managerial, infrastructural, suppliers, manufacturing, distribution, marketing, innovation). Financial resources are access to capital, which is cheaper for established, reputable firms; managerial resources are illustrated by football clubs moving from star players to dynamic teams.

Figures 1 and 2 and the continuation of the internal analysis. Figure 1 divides SWOT analysis into the internal environment (strengths and weaknesses, organisational functions) and the external environment (opportunities and threats in the competitor, industry and general environments). Figure 2 is a template listing nine internal factors (financial, managerial, infrastructural, suppliers, manufacturing, distribution channels, marketing, brand equity, innovation resources) against strengths, weaknesses and strategic action. The text continues with infrastructural resources, the computerised systems for finance, procurement, production, logistics and customer relationships and the platforms they run on, and begins on suppliers.

The remaining internal factors, resource similarity and the challenges of internal analysis. Suppliers are rated on range, quality, availability, lead times and responsiveness; manufacturing on plant, automation and flexibility; distribution on logistics and channel partners; marketing on research, product, pricing, channel and promotion; brand equity on reputation with stakeholders; and innovation on culture plus copyrights, patents and trademarks. When competitors have very similar resources, as mobile operators such as Vodafone and T-Mobile share network and handset suppliers, they tend to adopt similar strategies and engage in coopetition, growing the market together. A common mistake in internal analysis is listing every factor in which the firm is thought strong or weak, which is hard to turn into strategic action.

End of the internal-analysis challenges and the start of external analysis. Practitioners should keep only factors that bear on the intended source of competitive advantage, judged against competitors; hygiene, for instance, is a basic requirement rather than a strength in catering, pharmaceuticals or hospitals. External analysis covers variables beyond the organisation's control. The examples given are an opportunity, mobile-money transactions estimated to reach $1 trillion by 2015, and a threat, online reading overtaking print, which pushes publishers such as Wiley and Pearson toward mobile formats. External factors fall into three areas (Figure 3): the competitor environment (rivals' resources and capabilities, illustrated by Nokia's challengers), the industry environment (Porter's five forces), and the general environment (PEST and its variants).

Figure 3 and the implications of the industry environment. Figure 3 is a template of external factors against opportunities, threats and strategic action: the competitor environment (the same resource categories as the internal template), the industry environment (Porter's five forces: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power, buyer power) and the general environment (political, economic, socio-cultural, technological, legal, environmental, demographic, ethical, regulatory). In the text, the five forces determine competitors' business models and profitability. From the industrial-organisation perspective a firm should choose the markets that offer the best opportunities, which matter more than its internal resources; from the resource-based view it should find a position where it can influence or shield itself from the five forces.

Figure 4 and the general environment. Figure 4 is a worked example for a supermarket chain: a nearby hypermarket (risk of losing customers to lower prices), many new fruit and vegetable suppliers (lower prices), stricter HACCP rules (higher compliance costs), recession (lower demand or a shift to cheaper food), time-poor health-conscious families (demand for healthy ready meals), and online channels (wider market reach). The text argues that firms able to shape their industry, such as Microsoft, Apple with the iPod, iPhone and iPad, or the consortia behind GSM and 3G, earn above-average profits. It notes that SWOT's external review leans toward the resource-based view. General-environment analysis uses PEST-type dimensions, and opportunities and threats are specific to a business, so new communication technology threatens traditional tour operators but opens the market to new intermediaries. Sources of external information begin to be listed.

Sources of external information, cognitive inertia and the TOWS matrix, with Figure 5. Information comes from trade press, research reports and trade shows, and from staff who deal with the market, such as sales, customer care and procurement. Strategists' cognitive maps, shaped by experience, can ignore market signals in fast-changing industries, and this cognitive inertia can lead to decline unless it is regularly re-examined. Weihrich's TOWS matrix (Figure 5) derives tactical strategies from four pairings: WO (use opportunities to overcome weaknesses, for example a joint venture or subcontracting to obtain screen technology for tablets), SO (use strengths to exploit opportunities), ST (use strengths against threats) and WT (minimise weaknesses and avoid threats).

The rest of the TOWS strategies, a critique of SWOT and the bibliography. SO is illustrated by Apple's $140 billion cash balance in 2013, used to build its supply chain; ST by Microsoft's €561 million EU fine in 2013 over browser choice (€2.2 billion in EU fines over ten years), showing that a dominant firm must counter threats with caution; WT by the large tobacco companies' pre-emptive strategies against regulation and lawsuits. The authors' critique is that SWOT describes the current position but does not prescribe strategic action, so analysis should go beyond lists to cause and effect; combining it with the Balanced Scorecard and Quality Function Deployment has been proposed. They conclude that SWOT remains a useful tool for reviewing competitive position. The bibliography has six entries (Hitt and colleagues; Ip and Koo; McGee and colleagues; Sammut-Bonnici and McGee; Sirmon and colleagues; Weihrich and Cannice).
